claim: Internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs) mediate cap-independent translation of viral mRNAs.
source: Internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs) mediate cap-independent translation of viral mRNAs.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and references to prior work.

claim: Five ribosome structures were obtained from a single specimen using electron cryo-microscopy.
source: Using electron cryo-microscopy of a single specimen, we present five ribosome structures formed with the Taura syndrome virus IRES and translocase eEF2•GTP bound with sordarin.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that five structures were obtained from a single specimen, and this is supported by the methods and results sections.

claim: The IRES rearranges from extended to bent to extended conformations during translocation.
source: The IRES rearranges from extended to bent to extended conformations.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: IRES translocation involves inchworm-like movement.
source: This inchworm-like movement is coupled with ribosomal inter-subunit rotation and 40S head swivel.
evidence: The abstract describes the movement as 'inchworm-like' and this is elaborated in the results and discussion sections with structural evidence.

claim: eEF2 is attached to the 60S subunit and slides along the rotating 40S subunit to enter the A site.
source: eEF2, attached to the 60S subunit, slides along the rotating 40S subunit to enter the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The diphthamide-bearing tip of eEF2 at domain IV separates PKI from the decoding center.
source: Its diphthamide-bearing tip at domain IV separates the tRNA-mRNA-like pseudoknot I (PKI) of the IRES from the decoding center.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data in Figure 7.

claim: Separation of PKI from the decoding center unlocks 40S domains and facilitates head swivel.
source: This unlocks 40S domains, facilitating head swivel and biasing IRES translocation via hitherto-elusive intermediates with PKI captured between the A and P sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the discussion with structural evidence.

claim: Some viral mRNAs undergo cap-independent translation to efficiently compete with host mRNAs.
source: To efficiently compete with host mRNAs and engage in translation under stress, some viral mRNAs undergo cap-independent translation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work (Deforges et al. (2015), Jackson et al. (2010), Lozano and Martinez-Salas (2015)).

claim: An IRES is located at the 5' untranslated region of viral mRNA, preceding an open reading frame.
source: An IRES is located at the 5' untranslated region of the viral mRNA, preceding an open reading frame (ORF).
evidence: This is a standard definition stated in the introduction.

claim: IGR IRES-driven initiation does not involve initiator tRNAMet and initiation factors.
source: The IGR-IRES-driven initiation does not involve initiator tRNAMet and initiation factors (Jan et al., 2001; Sasaki and Nakashima, 1999; Wilson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: IGR IRESs represent the most streamlined mechanism of eukaryotic translation initiation.
source: As such, this group of IRESs represents the most streamlined mechanism of eukaryotic translation initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of the fact that IGR IRESs do not require initiator tRNA or initiation factors.

claim: IGR IRESs can initiate bacterial translation.
source: A recent demonstration of bacterial translation initiation by an IGR IRES (Colussi et al., 2015) indicates that the IRESs take advantage of conserved structural and dynamic properties of the ribosome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Colussi et al., 2015.

claim: IGR IRESs position the ORF by mimicking a translating ribosome bound with tRNA and mRNA.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of ribosome-bound TSV IRES (Koh et al., 2014) and CrPV IRES (Fernandez et al., 2014) revealed that IGR IRESs position the ORF by mimicking a translating ribosome bound with tRNA and mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: PKI of IGR IRESs mimics an A-site elongator tRNA interacting with an mRNA sense codon.
source: PKI of IGR IRESs therefore mimics an A-site elongator tRNA interacting with an mRNA sense codon, but not a P-site initiator tRNAMet and the AUG start codon.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on prior structural studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2014).

claim: For a cognate aminoacyl-tRNA to bind the first viral mRNA codon, PKI has to be translocated from the A site.
source: For a cognate aminoacyl-tRNA to bind the first viral mRNA codon, PKI has to be translocated from the A site, so that the first codon can be presented in the A site.
evidence: This is a logical inference stated in the introduction based on the mechanism of translation.

claim: Translocation of the IRES or tRNA-mRNA requires eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (eEF2).
source: Translocation of the IRES or tRNA-mRNA requires eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (eEF2) (Jan et al., 2003; Pestova and Hellen, 2003), a structural and functional homolog of the well-studied bacterial EF-G (Czworkowski et al., 1994; Evarsson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Intersubunit rotation of the small subunit relative to the large subunit is required for translocation.
source: First, studies of bacterial ribosomes showed that a ~10° rotation of the small subunit relative to the large subunit, known as intersubunit rotation, or ratcheting (Frank and Agrawal, 2000), is required for translocation (Horan and Noller, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work on bacterial ribosomes.

claim: Intersubunit rotation occurs spontaneously upon peptidyl transfer and is coupled with formation of hybrid tRNA states.
source: Intersubunit rotation occurs spontaneously upon peptidyl transfer, and is coupled with formation of hybrid tRNA states (Agirrezabala et al., 2008; Blanchard et al., 2004; Cornish et al., 2008; Ermolenko et al., 2007; Julián et al., 2008; Moazed and Noller, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The ribosome can undergo spontaneous, thermally-driven forward-reverse rotation.
source: The ribosome can undergo spontaneous, thermally-driven forward-reverse rotation (Cornish et al., 2008) that shifts the two tRNAs between the hybrid and 'classical' states while the anticodon stem loops remain non-translocated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Cornish et al., 2008.

claim: Binding of EF-G next to the A site and reverse rotation of the small subunit results in translocation of both ASLs on the small subunit.
source: Binding of EF-G next to the A site and reverse rotation of the small subunit results in translocation of both ASLs on the small subunit (Ermolenko and Noller, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Ermolenko and Noller, 2011.

claim: EF-G is thought to 'unlock' the pre-translocation ribosome.
source: EF-G is thought to 'unlock' the pre-translocation ribosome (Savelsbergh et al., 2003; Spirin, 1969), allowing movement of the 2tRNA•mRNA complex, however the structural details of this unlocking are not known.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations, but the manuscript notes that structural details are lacking.

claim: The head of the small subunit can rotate by up to ~20° around an axis nearly orthogonal to that of intersubunit rotation.
source: The head can rotate by up to ~20° around the axis nearly orthogonal to that of intersubunit rotation, in the absence of tRNA (Schuwirth et al., 2005) or in the presence of a single P/E tRNA and eEF2 (Taylor et al., 2007) or EF-G (Ratje et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: FRET data suggest that head swivel of the rotated small subunit facilitates EF-G-mediated movement of 2tRNA•mRNA.
source: Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) data suggest that head swivel of the rotated small subunit facilitates EF-G-mediated movement of 2tRNA•mRNA (Guo and Noller, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Guo and Noller, 2012.

claim: The head swivel was proposed to facilitate transition of the tRNA from the P to E site by widening a constriction between these sites.
source: The head swivel was proposed to facilitate transition of the tRNA from the P to E site by widening a constriction between these sites on the 30S subunit (Schuwirth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Schuwirth et al., 2005.

claim: Maximum-likelihood classification using FREALIGN identified five IRES-eEF2-bound ribosome structures within a single sample.
source: Maximum-likelihood classification using FREALIGN (Lyumkis et al., 2013) identified five IRES-eEF2-bound ribosome structures within a single sample (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the methods and figures.

claim: The five structures differ in the positions and conformations of ribosomal subunits, IRES RNA, and eEF2.
source: The structures differ in the positions and conformations of ribosomal subunits (Figures 1b and 2), IRES RNA (Figures 3 and 4) and eEF2 (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by multiple figures showing structural differences.

claim: PKI is partially withdrawn from the A site in Structure I.
source: Specifically, PKI is partially withdrawn from the A site in Structure I, and fully translocated to the P site in Structure V (Figure 4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: PKI is fully translocated to the P site in Structure V.
source: Specifically, PKI is partially withdrawn from the A site in Structure I, and fully translocated to the P site in Structure V (Figure 4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: Structures I to IV represent different positions of PKI between the A and P sites.
source: Thus Structures I to IV represent different positions of PKI between the A and P sites (Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting that these structures describe intermediate states of translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Structure V corresponds to the post-translocation state.
source: Structure V corresponds to the post-translocation state.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data showing PKI in the P site.

claim: Structure I comprises the most rotated ribosome conformation (~10°).
source: Structure I comprises the most rotated ribosome conformation (~10°), characteristic of pre-translocation hybrid-tRNA states.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements in Figure 2.

claim: From Structure I to V, the body of the small subunit undergoes backward (reverse) rotation.
source: From Structure I to V, the body of the small subunit undergoes backward (reverse) rotation (Figure 2b; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2b.

claim: Structures II and III are in mid-rotation conformations (~5°).
source: Structures II and III are in mid-rotation conformations (~5°).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: Structure IV adopts a slightly rotated conformation (~1°).
source: Structure IV adopts a slightly rotated conformation (~1°).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: Structure V is in a nearly non-rotated conformation (0.5°).
source: Structure V is in a nearly non-rotated conformation (0.5°), very similar to that of post-translocation ribosome-tRNA complexes (Gao et al., 2009; Korostelev et al., 2006; Selmer et al., 2006; Svidritskiy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements and citations.

claim: The head samples a mid-swiveled position in Structure I (12°).
source: The head samples a mid-swiveled position in Structure I (12°), then a highly-swiveled position in Structures II and III (17°) and a less swiveled position in Structure IV (14°).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements in Figure 2.

claim: The maximum head swivel is observed in the mid-rotated complexes II and III.
source: The maximum head swivel is observed in the mid-rotated complexes II and III, in which PKI transitions from the A to P site, while eEF2 occupies the A site partially.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: eEF2 is necessary for inducing or stabilizing the large head swivel of the 40S subunit characteristic for IRES translocation intermediates.
source: These observations suggest that eEF2 is necessary for inducing or stabilizing the large head swivel of the 40S subunit characteristic for IRES translocation intermediates.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data comparing structures with and without eEF2.

claim: In Structures I to IV, the L1.1 region, SL4, and SL5 contacts remain as in the initiation complex.
source: In Structures I to IV, these contacts remain as in the initiation complex (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1a.

claim: In Structure V, the density for SL5 is missing suggesting that SL5 is mobile.
source: In Structure V, however, the density for SL5 is missing suggesting that SL5 is mobile, while weak SL4 density suggests that SL4 is shifted along the surface of uS7, ~20 Å away from its initial position (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The shape of the IRES changes considerably from the initiation state to Structures I through V, from an extended to compact to extended conformation.
source: The shape of the IRES changes considerably from the initiation state to Structures I through V, from an extended to compact to extended conformation (Figure 4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: In the 80S•IRES initiation state, the A-site-bound PKI is separated from SL4 by almost 50 Å.
source: In the 80S•IRES initiation state (Koh et al., 2014), the A-site-bound PKI is separated from SL4 by almost 50 Å (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4 and a citation.

claim: In Structures I and II, the distance from PKI to SL4 shortens to ~35 Å.
source: In Structures I and II, the PKI is partially retracted from the A site and the distance from SL4 shortens to ~35 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: In Structures III and IV, the PKI domain approaches to within ~25 Å of SL4.
source: As PKI moves toward the P site in Structures III and IV, the PKI domain approaches to within ~25 Å of SL4.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: In Structure I, SL3 of the PKI domain is positioned between the A-site finger and the P site of the 60S subunit.
source: In Structure I, SL3 of the PKI domain is positioned between the A-site finger (nt 1008–1043 of 25S rRNA) and the P site of the 60S subunit, comprising helix 84 of 25S rRNA (nt. 2668–2687) and protein uL5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Loop 3 is poorly resolved in Structures I through IV, suggesting conformational flexibility.
source: This loop is poorly resolved in Structures I through IV, suggesting conformational flexibility in agreement with structural studies of the isolated PKI (Costantino et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2011) and biochemical studies of unbound IRESs (Jan and Sarnow, 2002; Pfingsten et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Structure V, loop 3 is bound in the 40S E site.
source: In Structure V, loop 3 is bound in the 40S E site and the backbone of loop 3 near the codon-like part of PKI (at nt. 6945–6946) interacts with R148 and R157 in β-hairpin of uS7.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Ordering of loop 3 suggests that this flexible region contributes to the stabilization of the PKI domain in the post-translocation state.
source: Ordering of loop 3 suggests that this flexible region contributes to the stabilization of the PKI domain in the post-translocation state.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Elongation factor eEF2 in all five structures is bound with GDP and sordarin.
source: Elongation factor eEF2 in all five structures is bound with GDP and sordarin (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5.

claim: ADP-ribosylation of eEF2 at the tip of domain IV or deletion of domain IV from EF-G abrogate translocation.
source: ADP-ribosylation of eEF2 at the tip of domain IV (Davydova and Ovchinnikov, 1990; Nygard and Nilsson, 1990) or deletion of domain IV from EF-G (Martemyanov and Gudkov, 1999; Rodnina et al., 1997) abrogate translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In post-translocation-like 80S•tRNA•eEF2 complexes, domain IV binds in the 40S A site.
source: In post-translocation-like 80S•tRNA•eEF2 complexes, domain IV binds in the 40S A site, suggesting direct involvement of domain IV in translocation of tRNA from the A to P site (Spahn et al., 2004a; Taylor et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GDP is bound in the GTPase center in all five structures.
source: GDP in our structures is bound in the GTPase center (Figures 5d, e and f) and sordarin is sandwiched between the β-platforms of domains III and V (Figures 5g and h), as in the structure of free eEF2•sordarin complex (Jorgensen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 5d, e, and f.

claim: Sordarin is sandwiched between the β-platforms of domains III and V.
source: GDP in our structures is bound in the GTPase center (Figures 5d, e and f) and sordarin is sandwiched between the β-platforms of domains III and V (Figures 5g and h), as in the structure of free eEF2•sordarin complex (Jorgensen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 5g and h.

claim: The global conformations of eEF2 are similar in all five structures (all-atom RMSD ≤ 2 Å).
source: The global conformations of eEF2 (Figure 5a) are similar in these structures (all-atom RMSD ≤ 2 Å), but the positions of eEF2 relative to the 40S subunit differ substantially as a result of 40S subunit rotation (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5a and structural measurements.

claim: From Structure I to V, eEF2 is rigidly attached to the GTPase-associated center of the 60S subunit.
source: From Structure I to V, eEF2 is rigidly attached to the GTPase-associated center of the 60S subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The GTPase-associated center comprises the P stalk and the sarcin-ricin loop.
source: The GTPase-associated center comprises the P stalk (L11 and L7/L12 stalk in bacteria) and the sarcin-ricin loop (SRL, nt 3012–3042).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a definition.

claim: The position of the P stalk remains unchanged from Structure I to V.
source: Although the P/L11 stalk is known to be dynamic (Korostelev et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2012), its position remains unchanged from Structure I to V: all-atom root-mean-square differences for the 25S rRNA of the P stalk (nt 1223–1286) are within 2.5 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: With respect to its position in the 80S•IRES complex in the absence of eEF2, the P stalk is shifted by ~13 Å toward the A site.
source: However, with respect to its position in the 80S•IRES complex in the absence of eEF2 and in the 80S•2tRNA•mRNA complex, the P stalk is shifted by ~13 Å toward the A site (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2d.

claim: There is an important local difference between Structure I and Structures II-V in switch loop I.
source: While the overall mode of this interaction is similar to that seen in 70S•EF-G crystal structures (Chen et al., 2013b; Gao et al., 2009; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013; 2014), there is an important local difference between Structure I and Structures II-V in switch loop I, as discussed below.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and elaborated later.

claim: Domain IV of eEF2 binds at the 40S A site in Structures I to V but the mode of interaction differs in each complex.
source: Domain IV of eEF2 binds at the 40S A site in Structures I to V but the mode of interaction differs in each complex (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6.

claim: Gradual entry of domain IV into the A site between Structures I and V is due to 40S subunit rotation and head swivel.
source: Because eEF2 is rigidly attached to the 60S subunit and does not undergo large inter-subunit rearrangements, gradual entry of domain IV into the A site between Structures I and V is due to 40S subunit rotation and head swivel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The tip of domain IV shifts by ~10 Å relative to the body and by ~20 Å relative to the swiveling head from Structure I to V.
source: eEF2 settles into the A site from Structure I to V, as the tip of domain IV shifts by ~10 Å relative to the body and by ~20 Å relative to the swiveling head.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: From Structure I to V, domains II and III of eEF2 migrate by ~10 Å along the 40S surface.
source: From Structure I to V, these central domains migrate by ~10 Å along the 40S surface (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6c.

claim: In Structure V, domain III is displaced as a result of interaction with uS12.
source: Comparison of eEF2 conformations reveals that in Structure V, domain III is displaced as a result of interaction with uS12, as discussed below.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and elaborated later.

claim: In Structure I, PKI is shifted toward the P site by ~3 Å relative to its position in the initiation complex.
source: In the fully rotated Structure I, PKI is shifted toward the P site by ~3 Å relative to its position in the initiation complex but maintains interactions with the partially swiveled head.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: C1274 of the 18S rRNA base pairs with the first nucleotide of the ORF immediately downstream of PKI.
source: At the head, C1274 of the 18S rRNA (C1054 in E. coli) base pairs with the first nucleotide of the ORF immediately downstream of PKI.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: C1274 provides a stacking platform for the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI and is defined as the foundation of the 'head A site'.
source: The C1274:G6953 base pair provides a stacking platform for the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI. We therefore define C1274 as the foundation of the 'head A site'.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a definition based on structural data.

claim: In Structure I, PKI does not contact the decoding-center nucleotides G577, A1755 and A1756.
source: In Structure I, PKI does not contact these nucleotides (Figures 2g and 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2g and 7.

claim: The position of eEF2 on the 40S subunit of Structure I is markedly distinct from those in Structures II to V.
source: The position of eEF2 on the 40S subunit of Structure I is markedly distinct from those in Structures II to V.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure I, the translocase interacts with the 40S body but does not contact the head.
source: The translocase interacts with the 40S body but does not contact the head (Figures 5b and 6a; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 5b and 6a.

claim: In Structure I, domain IV is partially engaged with the body A site.
source: Domain IV is partially engaged with the body A site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The tip of domain IV is wedged between PKI and decoding-center nucleotides A1755 and A1756 in Structure I.
source: The tip of domain IV is wedged between PKI and decoding-center nucleotides A1755 and A1756, which are bulged out of h44.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data in Figure 7.

claim: The tip of domain IV contains the histidine-diphthamide triad (H583, H694 and Diph699).
source: This tip contains the histidine-diphthamide triad (H583, H694 and Diph699), which interacts with the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI and A1756 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: Histidines 583 and 694 interact with the phosphate backbone of the anticodon-like strand at G6907 and C6908.
source: Histidines 583 and 694 interact with the phosphate backbone of the anticodon-like strand (at G6907 and C6908).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Diphthamide is a unique posttranslational modification conserved in archaeal and eukaryotic EF2.
source: Diphthamide is a unique posttranslational modification conserved in archaeal and eukaryotic EF2 (at residue 699 in S. cerevisiae) and involves addition of a ~7-Å long 3-carboxyamido-3-(trimethylamino)-propyl moiety to the histidine imidazole ring at CE1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a definition based on established knowledge.

claim: The trimethylamino end of Diph699 packs over A1756 in Structure I.
source: The trimethylamino end of Diph699 packs over A1756 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 replaces the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI in comparison with the initiation state.
source: Thus, in comparison with the initiation state, the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 replaces the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The conformation of the eEF2 GTPase center in Structure I resembles that of a GTP-bound translocase.
source: Unlike in Structures II to V, the conformation of the eEF2 GTPase center in Structure I resembles that of a GTP-bound translocase (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5e.

claim: Switch loop II carries the catalytic H108.
source: Switch loop II (aa 105–110), which carries the catalytic H108 (H92 in E. coli EF-G; (Cunha et al., 2013; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Koripella et al., 2015; Salsi et al., 2014) is well resolved in all five structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Switch loop I is resolved only in Structure I.
source: By contrast, switch loop I (aa 50–70 in S. cerevisiae eEF2) is resolved only in Structure I (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conformations of SWI and the GTPase center in Structure I are similar to those observed in ribosome-bound EF-Tu and EF-G in the presence of GTP analogs.
source: As such, the conformations of SWI and the GTPase center in general are similar to those observed in ribosome-bound EF-Tu (Voorhees et al., 2010) and EF-G (Pulk and Cate, 2013; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013) in the presence of GTP analogs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Structure II, PKI is further shifted along the 40S body, traversing ~4 Å toward the P site relative to Structure I.
source: In Structure II, relative to Structure I, PKI is further shifted along the 40S body, traversing ~4 Å toward the P site (Figures 2e, f, and g), while stacking on C1274 at the head A site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2e, f, and g.

claim: The intermediate position of PKI in Structure II is possible due to a large swivel of the head relative to the body.
source: Thus, the intermediate position of PKI is possible due to a large swivel of the head relative to the body, which brings the head A site close to the body P site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: In Structure II, domain IV of eEF2 is further entrenched in the A site by ~3 Å relative to the body and ~8 Å relative to the head.
source: Domain IV of eEF2 is further entrenched in the A site by ~3 Å relative to the body and ~8 Å relative to the head, preserving its interactions with PKI.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: In Structure II, the decoding center residues A1755 and A1756 are rearranged to pack inside helix 44.
source: The decoding center residues A1755 and A1756 are rearranged to pack inside helix 44, making room for eEF2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure III, PKI has translocated along the 40S body to the body P site.
source: The map allows placement of PKI at the body P site (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Thus, in Structure III, PKI has translocated along the 40S body, but the head remains fully swiveled so that PKI is between the head A and P sites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lower resolution of the map in Structure III suggests that PKI is somewhat destabilized in the vicinity of the body P site.
source: Lower resolution of the map in this region suggests that PKI is somewhat destabilized in the vicinity of the body P site in the absence of stacking with the foundations of the head A site (C1274) or P site (U1191).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the map quality.

claim: In Structure IV, the 40S subunit is almost non-rotated relative to the 60S subunit, and the 40S head is mid-swiveled.
source: In Structure IV, the 40S subunit is almost non-rotated relative to the 60S subunit, and the 40S head is mid-swiveled.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: In Structure IV, unwinding of the head moves the head P-site residue U1191 and body P-site residue C1637 closer together.
source: Unwinding of the head moves the head P-site residue U1191 and body P-site residue C1637 closer together, resulting in a partially restored 40S P site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure IV, PKI is partially accommodated in the P site.
source: Whereas C1637 forms a stacking platform for the last base pair of PKI, U1191 does not yet stack on PKI because the head remains partially swiveled. This renders PKI partially accommodated in the P site (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2g.

claim: In Structure IV, unwinding of the 40S head positions the head A site closer to the body A site.
source: Unwinding of the 40S head also positions the head A site closer to the body A site. This results in rearrangements of eEF2 interactions with the head, allowing eEF2 to advance further into the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: In Structure V, PKI is fully accommodated in the P site.
source: In the nearly non-rotated and non-swiveled ribosome conformation in Structure V closely resembling that of the post-translocation 80S•2tRNA•mRNA complex (Svidritskiy et al., 2014), PKI is fully accommodated in the P site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure V, the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI is stacked on P-site residues U1191 and C1637.
source: The codon-anticodon–like helix is stacked on P-site residues U1191 and C1637 (Figure 3d), analogous to stacking of the tRNA-mRNA helix (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 3d and 3e.

claim: In Structure V, protein uS12 is shifted along with the 40S body as a result of intersubunit rotation.
source: In Structure V, protein uS12 is shifted along with the 40S body as a result of intersubunit rotation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure V, uS12 forms extensive interactions with eEF2 domains II and III.
source: In this position, uS12 forms extensive interactions with eEF2 domains II and III. Specifically, the C-terminal tail of uS12 packs against the β-barrel of domain II, while the β-barrel of uS12 packs against helix A of domain III.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure V, the tip of helix A of domain III is shifted by ~5 Å relative to that in Structure I.
source: This shifts the tip of helix A of domain III (at aa 500) by ~5 Å (relative to that in Structure I) toward domain I.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: In Structure V, domain IV of eEF2 is fully accommodated in the A site.
source: Domain IV of eEF2 is fully accommodated in the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure V, the first codon of the open reading frame is positioned in the A site.
source: The first codon of the open reading frame is also positioned in the A site, with bases exposed toward eEF2 (Figure 7), resembling the conformations of the A-site codons in EF-G-bound 70S complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: In Structure V, the histidine-diphthamide tip is bound in the minor groove of the P-site codon-anticodon helix.
source: As in the preceding Structures, the histidine-diphthamide tip is bound in the minor groove of the P-site codon-anticodon helix.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In Structure V, Diph699 interacts with four out of six codon-anticodon nucleotides.
source: Diph699 slightly rearranges, relative to that in Structure I (Figure 7), and interacts with four out of six codon-anticodon nucleotides.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The structures represent the trajectory of eEF2-induced IRES translocation.
source: We propose that together with the previously reported initiation state (Koh et al., 2014), these structures represent the trajectory of eEF2-induced IRES translocation (shown as an animation in http://labs.umassmed.edu/korostelevlab/msc/iresmovie.gif and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Translocation of the TSV IRES on the 40S subunit globally resembles a step of an inchworm.
source: Translocation of the TSV IRES on the 40S subunit globally resembles a step of an inchworm (Figure 4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 4.

claim: At all steps of IRES translocation, the head of the IRES inchworm (L1.1 region) is supported by the mobile L1 stalk.
source: Notably, at all steps, the head of the IRES inchworm (L1.1 region) is supported by the mobile L1 stalk.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claim: Upon translocation, the GCU start codon is positioned in the A site, ready for interaction with Ala-tRNAAla upon eEF2 departure.
source: Upon translocation, the GCU start codon is positioned in the A site (Structure V), ready for interaction with Ala-tRNAAla upon eEF2 departure.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The presence of several translocation complexes in a single sample suggests that the structures represent equilibrium states of forward and reverse translocation of the IRES.
source: The presence of several translocation complexes in a single sample suggests that the structures represent equilibrium states of forward and reverse translocation of the IRES, which interconvert among each other.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the experimental design.

claim: Intergenic IRESs are prone to reverse translocation.
source: This is consistent with the observations that the intergenic IRESs are prone to reverse translocation. Specifically, biochemical toe-printing studies in the presence of eEF2•GTP identified IRES in a non-translocated position unless eEF1a•aa-tRNA is also present (Jan et al., 2003; Pestova and Hellen, 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: IRES translocation by eEF2 is futile: the IRES returns to the A site upon releasing eEF2•GDP unless an amino-acyl tRNA enters the A site.
source: These findings indicate that IRES translocation by eEF2 is futile: the IRES returns to the A site upon releasing eEF2•GDP unless an amino-acyl tRNA enters the A site and blocks IRES back-translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of prior biochemical studies.

claim: Intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site.
source: Specifically, intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site, while the head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
source: Specifically, intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site, while the head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Reverse intersubunit rotation facilitates full docking of eEF2 in the A site.
source: Reverse intersubunit rotation from Structure I to V shifts the translocation tunnel (the tunnel between the A, P and E sites) toward eEF2, which is rigidly attached to the 60S subunit. This allows eEF2 to move into the A site. As such, reverse intersubunit rotation facilitates full docking of eEF2 in the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: eEF2 appears to directly force PKI out of the A site.
source: Because the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 (H583, H694 and Diph699) attaches to the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI, eEF2 appears to directly force PKI out of the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The fully swiveled conformations of Structures II and III represent the mid-point of translocation.
source: The fully swiveled conformations of Structures II and III represent the mid-point of translocation, in which PKI relocates between the head A site and body P site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The structures provide the first high-resolution view of the dynamics of a ribosomal translocase inferred from an ensemble of structures sampled under uniform conditions.
source: To our knowledge, our work provides the first high-resolution view of the dynamics of a ribosomal translocase that is inferred from an ensemble of structures sampled under uniform conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The first role of eEF2 in translocation is to directly shift PKI out of the A site upon spontaneous reverse intersubunit rotation.
source: As discussed above, the first role is to directly shift PKI out of the A site upon spontaneous reverse intersubunit rotation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The tip of domain IV docks next to PKI, with diphthamide 699 fit into the minor groove of the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI.
source: In our structures, the tip of domain IV docks next to PKI, with diphthamide 699 fit into the minor groove of the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claim: This arrangement rationalizes inactivation of eEF2 by diphtheria toxin.
source: This arrangement rationalizes inactivation of eEF2 by diphtheria toxin, which catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the diphthamide (reviewed in Collier, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: The bulky ADP-ribosyl moiety at the NE2 position would disrupt the interaction of diphthamide with PKI, rendering eEF2 unable to bind to the A site.
source: The enzyme ADP-ribosylates the NE2 atom of the imidazole ring, which in our structures interacts with the first two residues of the anticodon-like strand of PKI. The bulky ADP-ribosyl moiety at this position would disrupt the interaction, rendering eEF2 unable to bind to the A site (Nygard and Nilsson, 1990) and/or stalled on ribosomes in a non-productive conformation (Bermek, 1976; Davydova and Ovchinnikov, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: Positively-charged patches of eEF2 slide over rRNA of the 40S body and head.
source: Positively-charged patches of domains II and III (R391, K394, R433, R510) and IV (K613, R617, R609, R631, K651) slide over rRNA of the 40S body (h5) and head (h18 and h33/h34), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claim: Sliding of eEF2 involves reorganization of electrostatic, perhaps isoenergetic interactions.
source: Thus, sliding of eEF2 involves reorganization of electrostatic, perhaps isoenergetic interactions, echoing those implied in extraordinarily fast ribosome inactivation rates by the small-protein ribotoxins (Korennykh et al., 2006) and in fast protein association and diffusion along DNA (Givaty and Levy, 2009; Gorman et al., 2010; Halford, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: The second key function of the translocase is 'unlocking' of intrasubunit rearrangements required for step-wise translocation of PKI on the small subunit.
source: Comparison of our structures with the 80S•IRES initiation structure reveals the structural basis for the second key function of the translocase: 'unlocking' of intrasubunit rearrangements that are required for step-wise translocation of PKI on the small subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: eEF2 induces head swivel by 'unlocking' the head-body interactions.
source: Our structures suggest that eEF2 induces head swivel by 'unlocking' the head-body interactions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 is wedged between A1755 and A1756 and PKI at an early pre-translocation step.
source: Structure I demonstrates that at an early pre-translocation step, the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 is wedged between A1755 and A1756 and PKI.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data from Structure I.

claim: Destabilization of PKI at the body A site allows PKI to detach from the body A site upon spontaneous reverse 40S body rotation.
source: This destabilization allows PKI to detach from the body A site upon spontaneous reverse 40S body rotation, while maintaining interactions with the head A site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The histidine-diphthamide-induced disengagement of PKI from A1755 and A1756 provides the structural definition for the 'unlocking' mode of eEF2 action.
source: The histidine-diphthamide-induced disengagement of PKI from A1755 and A1756 therefore provides the structural definition for the 'unlocking' mode of eEF2 action.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Both PKI and eEF2 passively migrate into the P and A site, respectively, during spontaneous 40S body rotation and head swivel.
source: In summary, our structures are consistent with a model of eEF2-induced translocation in which both PKI and eEF2 passively migrate into the P and A site, respectively, during spontaneous 40S body rotation and head swivel, the latter being allowed by 'unlocking' of the A site by eEF2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Thermal fluctuations of the 40S head domain are sufficient for translocation along the energetically flat trajectory.
source: Observation of different PKI conformations sampling a range of positions between the A and P sites in the presence of eEF2•GDP implies that thermal fluctuations of the 40S head domain are sufficient for translocation along the energetically flat trajectory.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: In the fully-rotated pre-translocation-like Structure I, switch loop I interacts with helix 14 of the 18S rRNA.
source: In the fully-rotated pre-translocation-like Structure I, an additional interaction exists. Here, switch loop I interacts with helix 14 (415CAAA418) of the 18S rRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claim: The fully rotated 40S subunit of the pre-translocation ribosome provides an interaction surface for binding of the GTP-bound translocase.
source: We conclude that unlike other conformations of the ribosome, the fully rotated 40S subunit of the pre-translocation ribosome provides an interaction surface, complementing the P stalk and SRL, for binding of the GTP-bound translocase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The shift of domain III by uS12 initiates intra-domain rearrangements in eEF2.
source: We propose that the shift of domain III by uS12 initiates intra-domain rearrangements in eEF2, which unstack the β-platform of domain III from that of domain V.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Structure V captures a 'pre-unstacking' state due to stabilization of the interface between domains III and V by sordarin.
source: As we discuss below, Structure V captures a 'pre-unstacking' state due to stabilization of the interface between domains III and V by sordarin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Density maps clearly show GDP and Mg2+ in each structure.
source: Although our complex was assembled using eEF2•GTP, density maps clearly show GDP and Mg2+ in each structure (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 5g.

claim: Sordarin stalls eEF2 on the ribosome in the GDP-bound form, i.e. following GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
source: Our structures therefore indicate that sordarin stalls eEF2 on the ribosome in the GDP-bound form, i.e. following GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Sordarin acts to prevent full reverse rotation and release of eEF2•GDP by stabilizing the interdomain interface.
source: We propose that sordarin acts to prevent full reverse rotation and release of eEF2•GDP by stabilizing the interdomain interface and thus blocking uS12-induced disengagement of domain III from domain V.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: tRNA and IRES translocations occur via the same general trajectory.
source: First, we propose that tRNA and IRES translocations occur via the same general trajectory.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The intermediate locations of the elusive A-to-P-site translocating tRNA are similar to those of PKI in our structures.
source: Overall, these correlations suggest that the intermediate locations of the elusive A-to-P-site translocating tRNA are similar to those of PKI in our structures.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior work.

claim: Unlocking involves separation of the codon-anticodon helix from the decoding center residues by the protruding tip of eEF2/EF-G.
source: Unlocking involves separation of the codon-anticodon helix from the decoding center residues by the protruding tip of eEF2/EF-G (Figure 7), occurring in the fully rotated ribosome at an early pre-translocation step.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The head swivel brings the head A site to the body P site, allowing a step-wise conveying of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
source: In addition to the 'gate-opening' role, we now show that the head swivel brings the head A site to the body P site, allowing a step-wise conveying of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The similar populations of particles in the reconstructions suggest that the intermediate translocation states sample several energetically similar and interconverting conformations.
source: Finally, the similar populations of particles (within a 2X range) in our 80S•IRES•eEF2 reconstructions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggest that the intermediate translocation states sample several energetically similar and interconverting conformations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The energy landscape of translocation is not completely flat and contains local minima for transient positions of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
source: Our findings implicate, however, that the energy landscape is not completely flat and contains local minima for transient positions of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The TSV IRES structurally and dynamically represents a chimera of the 2tRNA•mRNA translocating complex.
source: The cryo-EM structures demonstrate that the TSV IRES structurally and dynamically represents a chimera of the 2tRNA•mRNA translocating complex (A/P-tRNA • P/E-tRNA • mRNA).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The IRES lacks three out of six tRNA-like domains involved in tRNA translocation.
source: A large structural difference between the IRES and the 2tRNA•mRNA complex exists, however, in that the IRES lacks three out of six tRNA-like domains involved in tRNA translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The uniformity of ribosome dynamics underscores the idea that translocation is an inherent and structurally-optimized property of the ribosome.
source: The uniformity of ribosome dynamics underscores the idea that translocation is an inherent and structurally-optimized property of the ribosome, supported also by translocation activity in the absence of the elongation factor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: Intergenic IRESs represent a striking example of convergent molecular evolution.
source: Intergenic IRESs, in turn, represent a striking example of convergent molecular evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Viral mRNAs have evolved to adopt an atypical structure to employ the inherent ribosome dynamics.
source: Viral mRNAs have evolved to adopt an atypical structure to employ the inherent ribosome dynamics, to be able to hijack the host translational machinery in a simple fashion.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: 80S ribosomes used in this study were prepared from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303.
source: 80S ribosomes used in this study were prepared from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303 as described previously (Ben-Shem et al., 2011; Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: C-terminally His6-tagged eEF2 was produced in yeast TKY675 cells.
source: C-terminally His6-tagged eEF2 was produced in yeast TKY675 cells obtained from Terri Goss Kinzy.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Cryo-EM data were collected in movie mode on an FEI Krios microscope operating at 300 kV.
source: Cryo-EM data were collected in movie mode on an FEI Krios microscope (FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a K2 Summit direct detector (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA) operating in super-resolution mode with pixel size of 0.82 Å per super-resolution pixel.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 1,105,737 two-dimensional images of ribosomes were picked automatically.
source: 1,105,737 two-dimensional images of ribosomes (termed 'particles') were picked automatically, extracted into 256 x 256 boxes and converted to MRC/CCP4 format with a corresponding list of micrograph numbers and defocus values for input to FREALIGN v9 (Lyumkis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: FREALIGN v9 was used for refinement, classification and 3D reconstruction of all ribosome structures.
source: FREALIGN v9 was used for refinement, classification and 3D reconstruction of all ribosome structures.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The structures have average resolutions of 3.5 to 4.2 Å.
source: This approach revealed five 80S•IRES•eEF2•GDP structures at average resolutions of 3.5 to 4.2 Å, sufficient to locate IRES domains and to resolve individual residues in the core regions of the ribosome and eEF2 (Figures 3c,d, and 5f,h; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), including the post-translational modification diphthamide 699 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.
